Hierarchy. The ordering of individuals or groups in a ranked structure where some occupy higher positions with greater authority, prestige, or control than others. Found in human societies from small bands to complex organizations, hierarchy enables coordination and decision-making by creating clear channels of communication and command. It is both a feature of social organization and a psychological reality—humans readily form hierarchical relationships.

Hierarchies exist across scales. Within families, parents rank above children. In organizations, managers rank above employees. Military structures, academic institutions, and entire societies divided by class or caste all embody hierarchy. Social hierarchy in early human societies likely arose with permanent settlements and agriculture, as surplus resources enabled some individuals to accumulate power and command others. Hunter-gatherer bands are comparatively egalitarian. Hierarchies are not purely coercive. They often rest on legitimacy—the belief that authority holders have the right to command—which makes compliance voluntary rather than forced.

Status and rank are the perceptual dimensions of hierarchy. People recognize their position relative to others and adjust behavior accordingly. Hierarchy can be fluid, achieved through merit or temporary advantage, or rigid, inherited through birth as in caste systems. Most societies blend both mechanisms. Experimental psychology, including Stanley Milgram's obedience studies, revealed how strongly people defer to authority figures perceived as legitimate occupants of hierarchical positions. Hierarchies facilitate coordination in large groups. With clear command structures, decisions can cascade downward and information can flow upward, solving problems that egalitarian groups find difficult without formal organization. Dominance hierarchies, observed in primates and other species, suggest humans may have evolutionary predispositions to establish ranked relationships, though culture dramatically shapes how hierarchies form and persist.
